tier_reason: The paper (arXiv 2410.19146, a preprint; no peer-reviewed venue seen) could not be opened: arxiv.org fails with ENOTFOUND here, and two searches found no code repository. The numbers come from search snippets only, so the wave-14 snippet-only rule caps it at C, with compiler, flags, algorithm equivalence and mechanism all unknown.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Per search snippets of the arXiv paper (paper not opened): Rust was at least 1.6x as fast as the C++ version in the smaller cases, and up to 5.6x faster on the large mesh on the EPYC machine; a parallel Rust version improved performance further. No per-case runtimes were seen.
corrections.workload: A re-implementation, from C++ to Rust, of a laser-plasma interaction simulation of Cross Beam Energy Transfer (CBET, energy transfer where high-intensity laser beams cross in a plasma), run on test cases with different mesh sizes on more than one machine (one is an AMD EPYC system), plus a parallel Rust version. A snippet also mentions a comparison with an interpreted-language (MATLAB) version.
corrections.hardware: Includes an AMD EPYC machine (model not seen; snippet only)
corrections.stars_or_usage: arXiv 2410.19146 (submitted 24 October 2024, physics.comp-ph), University of Rochester; discussed on lobste.rs; no peer-reviewed venue found
corrections.caveats: Snippet only: arxiv.org (abs, html and pdf) is blocked here (ENOTFOUND) and two searches found no public code for either the C++ or the Rust version. Compiler versions, optimisation flags, algorithm equivalence and the reason for the speedup are unknown, so same_algorithm, same_opt_level and why_faster stay null. A rewrite by the same group can carry design changes (data layout, algorithm fixes) that make it a rewrite effect rather than a language effect, and a 1.6x-5.6x gap between equally optimised C++ and Rust is unusual. Contrast: the ASE 2022 study 'Towards Understanding the Runtime Performance of Rust' (Zhang et al.) reports Rust 1.77x slower than C on average for same-algorithm micro-benchmarks, and 'Is Rust C++-fast?' (arXiv 2209.09127) reports Rust similar to C++ with a minor disadvantage. The paper is an arXiv preprint, so it is not counted as peer-reviewed.

notes: The record is accurate as a snippet-only lead and stays at C. I added the arXiv URL (not opened) and the snippet detail of at least 1.6x on small cases and 5.6x on the large mesh on EPYC. Shortcomings for the orchestrator: no code, paper unreadable here, flags and algorithm equivalence unknown, a likely rewrite effect, and a preprint only. Worth a paper-access retier from an environment where arxiv.org is reachable.

tier_reason: Upgraded from C. The peer-reviewed Nature Methods 2023 paper (abstract seen via snippet: >20x faster than FastANI on fragmented MAGs) has a public benchmark repo, bluenote-1577/skani-test, whose time_results.sh and time_2328_results.sh run skani, FastANI 1.33 and Mash 2.3 (bioconda pins in env.yml) under /bin/time -v, with the outputs checked into times/. It is not A because no CPU model or compiler flags are given.

corrections.baseline: FastANI 1.33 (C++) and Mash 2.3 (C++), bioconda builds pinned in skani-test/env.yml
corrections.claimed_speedup: README: sketching about 3x faster than Mash, querying about 25x faster than FastANI but slower than Mash; v0.4.0 (October 2026) claims about 2x faster than v0.3. Paper abstract (snippet only): >20x faster than FastANI on fragmented, incomplete MAGs. Paper benchmark repo skani-test, /bin/time outputs at 50 threads (derived from page data): all-vs-all on 195 MAGs, skani triangle 3.30 s vs FastANI 2:58.96 (54x wall; 154.75 s vs 7142.43 s user, 46x); E. coli D3 database query, skani search 4.17 s (plus 3.55 s sketching) vs FastANI 2:44.50 (39x query-only, 21x including sketching); RefSeq all-vs-all, skani sketch 3.10 s plus triangle 11.38 s vs FastANI 3:02:24 (about 750x). Against Mash: skani sketching 3.55 s vs 18.19 s on D3 and 3.10 s vs 14.79 s on RefSeq (about 5x), but Mash dist on D3 takes 0.26 s vs skani search 4.17 s (skani 16x slower), and Mash triangle on the 195 MAGs takes 0.55 s vs 3.30 s.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: skani: prebuilt binary checked into skani-test (cargo release build; flags not stated). FastANI 1.33 (fastani=1.33=h0fdf51a_1) and Mash 2.3 (mash=2.3=ha9a2dd8_3) from bioconda, build flags those of the bioconda recipes.
corrections.hardware: CPU model not stated; 50 threads (/bin/time reports 3500-4950% CPU)
corrections.stars_or_usage: 265 stars, 15 forks; Nature Methods 2023 paper (doi 10.1038/s41592-023-02018-3); bioconda package; pyskani Python bindings by a third party
corrections.caveats: The speedup is algorithmic, not a language effect: skani does approximate mapping with sparse chaining of k-mer seeds and no base-level alignment, while FastANI uses Mashmap-style mapping of 3 kb fragments, so same_algorithm is false and the Rust-vs-C++ question is not answered. skani is slower than Mash at querying (16x on D3, 6x on the 195-MAG triangle) and only beats it at sketching. The timings come from the paper-era binary in skani-test, not the current v0.4.0. No CPU model is given, and the FastANI and Mash builds are bioconda defaults. The RefSeq row compares outputs filtered differently (skani -E edge list vs FastANI full output), so the ~750x figure is indicative only. The skani README says a C compiler is needed to build (C dependency). The README's 25x figure has no raw numbers on the README page itself. The wave-14 category is a poor fit, since the win comes from the method, not the language.

notes: Upgraded to B with verdict confirm: the peer-reviewed paper's public benchmark repo (skani-test) holds scripts and /bin/time outputs showing skani 21x-54x faster than FastANI 1.33 at 50 threads, but no CPU model. Shortcomings: an algorithmic win, not a language one (different method from FastANI); slower than Mash for querying; paper-era binary; CPU model absent. baseline_in_list corrected to false, since FastANI and Mash are not in the verified lists.

tier_reason: First-party README table produced by public code (tests/bench.nim, with benchy) and a stated Nim command line, but no CPU model, no C compiler or version, and an unknown build of the libsnappy.dll that serves as the Google Snappy baseline, so not A.

corrections.baseline: Google Snappy (C++), called through its C API (snappy_compress, snappy_uncompress, snappy_validate_compressed_buffer) from a prebuilt libsnappy.dll loaded by the nimsnappy wrapper (version and build flags unknown; the wrapper says it tracks 1.1.3). Also Andi Kleen's snappy-c (C), compiled from source into the benchmark through the nimsnappyc wrapper's {.compile.} pragma. The pure-Nim status-im/nim-snappy is the fourth column.
corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 'performs significantly better in all cases than alternatives'. Table, avg ms per compress-plus-uncompress round trip (derived ratios from page data). Against Google Snappy via nimsnappy: alice29.txt 0.513 vs 0.599 (1.17x), asyoulik.txt 0.451 vs 0.529 (1.17x), html_x_4 0.534 vs 0.559 (1.05x), kppkn.gtb 0.435 vs 0.523 (1.20x), lcet10.txt 1.380 vs 1.599 (1.16x), plrabn12.txt 1.898 vs 2.237 (1.18x), urls.10K 1.574 vs 1.842 (1.17x); slower on fireworks.jpg 0.015 vs 0.011, geo.protodata 0.106 vs 0.101 and paper-100k.pdf 0.041 vs 0.017, html 0.128 vs 0.127 (tie). Against snappy-c via nimsnappyc, faster on all 11 files by 1.10x (plrabn12.txt 1.898 vs 2.092) to 1.42x (geo.protodata 0.106 vs 0.150). Against status-im/nim-snappy it is slower on fireworks.jpg (0.015 vs 0.011) and paper-100k.pdf (0.041 vs 0.020). So 'all cases' holds only against snappy-c.
corrections.workload: Snappy benchmark corpus (alice29.txt, asyoulik.txt, fireworks.jpg, geo.protodata, html, html_x_4, kppkn.gtb, lcet10.txt, paper-100k.pdf, plrabn12.txt, urls.10K). tests/bench.nim times one compress plus one uncompress of the whole file per benchy timeIt sample, with 1000 samples (x1000). The README header's '100 compress-uncompress cycles' does not match the current code.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: nim c --gc:arc -d:release -r tests/bench.nim (README still says tests/benchmark.nim, which is now 404). Nim's release config compiles both its generated C and the {.compile.}'d snappy-c with the same backend C compiler (gcc/clang -O3, vcc /O2 per Nim's config/nim.cfg), and supersnappy turns checks off in release builds. The backend compiler and version are not stated, and the build of the libsnappy.dll used for Google Snappy is unknown.
corrections.hardware: Not stated (a Windows machine, judging by the .\tests path and libsnappy.dll)
corrections.caveats: Weak entry. Nim compiles to C, so this is a C-versus-C comparison and no language effect. The cleanest comparison is against snappy-c, built by the same C compiler at the same flags, which supersnappy beats on all 11 files by 1.10-1.42x; but the nimsnappyc wrapper calls snappy_init_env/snappy_free_env (allocating the hash table) on every compress, which inflates small-file times. Against Google Snappy the nimsnappy wrapper runs a full snappy_validate_compressed_buffer pass before every uncompress, and newString zero-fills both output buffers, so the C++ baseline does extra work; even so supersnappy wins only 16-20 percent on text, ties html and loses on fireworks.jpg, geo.protodata and paper-100k.pdf (2.4x slower on paper-100k.pdf). The libsnappy.dll version and flags are unknown (the wrapper says it tracks snappy 1.1.3, a 2015 release), no hardware is stated, and the README's 'all cases' claim is contradicted by its own table. The code credits snappy-c as its main influence.
corrections.why_faster: Implementation and harness, not language: supersnappy is a Snappy port (influenced by snappy-c) with Nim checks off in release, 32/64-bit word loads and table-driven tag decoding, compiled to C by the same compiler as the snappy-c baseline; against Google Snappy, the nimsnappy wrapper adds a validation pass before every uncompress.

notes: Confirmed at C with corrections. Google Snappy (wave 9 list) is the baseline, so baseline_in_list is now true. nimsnappy is confirmed to wrap Google's C++ snappy through its C API (snappy_validate_compressed_buffer, no env argument), not the C port. Shortcomings: wins only on text-like files against an extra-pass FFI wrapper of an old, unknown libsnappy.dll build; slower on 3 files; no hardware; Nim compiles to C, so no language effect; README's 'all cases' claim contradicted; benchmark path in README stale.
